lesson_title: Steel Wool on Fire: Reaction Rates
hook_text: A steel nail just glows in a flame. Steel WOOL bursts into sparks. Same steel. Why?
clip_script: Hold a steel nail in a flame and it glows, sulks, and does nothing. Hold fine steel wool in the same flame and it erupts in a shower of sparks. Same steel. Same flame. So what changed? Surface. A nail hides almost all of its particles deep inside, where oxygen can never touch them. Steel wool is nearly ALL outside — millions of exposed particles, all available for collision at once. And collisions are the whole game. Chemistry only happens when particles smash together hard enough — at or above the activation energy — and square-on. Chemists call those the effective collisions, and reaction rate is just effective collisions per second. Once you see that, every trick works. Stronger acid? More particles bumping per second. Heat it up? Now far MORE of the bumps hit hard enough to count — that is why warmth is chemistry's strongest lever. Add a catalyst? It lowers the bar itself, so gentler bumps score, and the catalyst walks away untouched, ready to do it again. One sentence unlocks the whole topic: more counting bumps per second. The nail never stood a chance — it kept its particles hidden.
visual_style: Macro shot energy: a glowing nail versus steel wool erupting in sparks; zoom into a bumper-car floor of particles where soft taps fizzle grey and hard square hits flash green; a bar labelled activation energy dropping as a catalyst slides in.
mood: Fiery and kinetic, with a satisfying one-sentence payoff.
pacing: Spark-shower cold open, rapid-fire factor montage, slow zoom on the falling activation bar, punchline sentence at the end.
